item.title: Playing Russian roulette with Pakistani rain
item.description:
Sulaiman, a school teacher in Buner, lives in a pocket of Pakistan hemmed in between Mardan, Swat and Swabi, where life is village and mountain stream and the fame of a valley charming and fertile. Climate ruin was an affliction reserved for places with mighty rivers such as the Swat or the Kunar. It made sense because Buner had none of these. Just sweet little springs trickling softly through the rocks.

That perception was pulverised on August 15, 2025.

It began as the sort of unassuming Friday that tricks you into believing you have the upper hand on the day. At 8:30 AM, Sulaiman could hear the rain tapping on the roof as he buttoned his shalwar kameez, one of the finer sets reserved for Jummah, before heading out. Within an hour, however, Nature lost its temper and dumped a cloudburst into the mountain-ringed basin.

From the classroom window, he saw a clear ribbon of a stream change into a slurry of liquefied soil. The brown tide smothered houses and shops, sucking cars, trucks, fleeing villagers and everything within the line of sight into its soup. Sulaiman hurriedly dialled his brother at their 33-room ancestral home where the entire family lived. The phone was picked up at the third ring, but before a word could be exchanged, the line went dead.

That day, out of 27 members of his family, 24 had died. An entire lineage and a collective loss estimated at over Rs 210 million were wiped out in the time it took Sulaiman to teach a single class. The survivors waded into the debris to pull bodies from the mud before any help arrived. It took over a week to find the last one.

What incenses Sulaiman the most is the divide between Pakistan’s urban centres and its margins. “We weren’t even asking for a day’s notice,” he says. “If we had received a single alert just 30 minutes before the cloudburst, we could have run up the mountain slopes and taken shelter at the higher houses.” So many lives could have been saved.

Nearly a year later, charities have helped rebuild basic shelter but the terrain remains glutted with stone, and the fields of maize and wheat ruined. Children returned to school but burdened by trauma that resurfaces whenever dark storm clouds gather over the peaks.

Headline after headline has been sounding the alarm. Here’s one that did the rounds last month: Nationwide deaths this monsoon cross 100; more rain likely in the country’s upper parts from July 29. While climate change gets most of the blame, the crisis is equally driven by flawed weather forecasting.

Goliath and Davids

As disaster and climate change specialist Fatima Yamin puts it, the problem is not the availability of information or its lack thereof; it is how it is conveyed to Pakistanis across the country. Broadcasting a storm warning on PTV or flooding a federal Twitter (X) handle does little for a villager in Bagrot Valley at 15,000 feet, or a family living in the parts of Jacobabad that are off the grid. “Not everyone has a TV,” she says, recalling the 2022 image of a family stranded in the middle of a roaring Swat river.

“Where are you sending these warnings? If the prediction of a weather event is that severe, it should be sent as text messages in a language the recipients will understand, echoed over local radio stations in native dialects, and posted on roadside addas and bus stops.” The academic posturing needs to be stripped away so citizens know what actually matters: Will water rise in their locality, on their street, outside their front door, in the next hour?

When a meteorological anomaly brews over a region, the Pakistan Meteorological Department (PMD) generates macro-level predictions. These turn into bulletins that navigate a series of channels to take the form of jargon-laden press releases that at times even disaster scientists struggle to translate, let alone a farmer in Sindh.

The story of weather forecasting in Pakistan is one of a state-backed Goliath equipped with global telecommunications networks, satellite feeds, and Doppler radars, against independent Davids armed with online global weather models, social media pages, and an appetite for public engagement.

To forecast, you have to be intimate with the terrain

To understand why our skies are notoriously difficult to predict, it is helpful to know the inner workings of the Pakistan Meteorological Department (PMD) as revealed by two experts: Dr Ghulam Rasul, its former director-general, and Dr Sardar Sarfaraz, a former Chief Meteorologist.

When Pakistan emerged on the map in 1947, it inherited a network of just nine meteorological observatories. Today, the PMD operates over 100 stations dotted across the country’s diverse climatic zones to study three distinct scientific domains: meteorology, hydrology, and seismology.

To capture the sky’s moods, the department deploys a web of instruments. The stations measure air temperature, wind speed and direction, atmospheric pressure, soil temperature across several depths, hourly rainfall, and visual cloud dynamics. The vertical atmospheric profiling is done by helium-filled weather balloons which release radiosondes or battery-powered telemetry devices that transmit atmospheric parameters every 100 meters as they climb into the upper atmosphere until they burst. Japan has funded Doppler radars in Karachi and Islamabad (alongside older but operational units in Lahore and smaller X, S, and C-band radars across the country) that cover 85 per cent of Pakistan’s landmass. Combined with geostationary satellite feeds, polar-orbiting satellite images, and oceanographic buoys tracking sea surface temperatures, these instruments feed volumes of data into numerical weather prediction models run on high-powered computers.

Crucially, as both experts emphasise, PMD belongs to an exclusive global fraternity. Through the World Meteorological Organisation’s Global Telecommunication System, PMD exchanges real-time upper air and surface data with national services in India, Bangladesh, Japan, and beyond. It is a vast, proprietary data pipeline that no independent forecaster can directly tap into.

Despite this formidable technological array, weather predictions, time and again, fail. Sarfaraz explains why. “Atmospheric science, unlike natural science, is a science of probability and uncertainty where 2 plus 2 don’t always make 4. Sometimes the answer is 5, and sometimes 3.”

He points out that the fundamental nature of the atmosphere is non-linear and inherently chaotic. Computerised numerical weather prediction models rely on physical and mathematical assumptions that do not always match the messy realities of nature. For instance, models generally assume a standard atmospheric lapse rate that temperature drops uniformly by 6 degree celsius per kilometer as you go up. In reality, the upward profile of the atmosphere is erratic; it can shift by 4 degree celsius one day and over 7 degree celsius the next. When initial parameters are off even slightly, computerised models compound these tiny errors over time.

Moreover, accuracy depends heavily on the forecast horizon. Short-range forecast (24–72 hours) has high precision, with typically 90pc or higher accuracy rate. With medium-range (3–7 days), accuracy begins to degrade as model assumptions warp over time. When it comes to long-range forecasts (15 days to 3 months), it drops significantly, often below 70pc, particularly in Pakistan where complex topography dictates abrupt micro-climatic shifts. Added to this are physical data gaps. While 100 observatories sound impressive, Sarfaraz notes that ideally, an observation data point is needed every 50 kilometers and massive blind spots persist over far-flung regions in the country.

There is an art to forecasting that raw computational horsepower cannot replicate: local terrain knowledge.

Global numerical models produced by European or American agencies often struggle to parse localised regional dynamics. Rasul highlights a classic example: tropical cyclones steaming across the Arabian Sea toward the coast of Sindh. When this happens, Western computer models are quick to predict a direct strike on Karachi. However, seasoned local meteorologists know the terrain dynamics that routinely divert these cyclones eastward toward the Rann of Kutch or Gujarat in India.

“A forecaster coming from Islamabad to Karachi to predict its weather would be confused by the city’s skies, where clouds form daily only to dissolve without rain,” he says. “To forecast a place, you have to be intimate with its terrain.”

Predicting severe weather, such as the formation of Cumulonimbus clouds that trigger hailstorms, lightning, and dangerous aviation downdrafts, requires reading colour-coded Doppler radar echoes alongside rising thermal air currents. This is where institutional memory and human intuition come in and interpret what the computer screens output.

The independent weathermen

The stories behind Pakistan’s leading private forecasters could not be more different from the traditional academic-to-bureaucrat pipeline.

Jawad Memon’s entry into meteorology started 15 years ago as a passion project. All he had in his arsenal was a newly installed Wi-Fi connection at home, an obsession with thunderstorms, and hours of self-guided internet research. Memon began sharing informal predictions on social media. This hobby morphed into Weather Updates PK, a platform whose forecasts are routinely picked up by TV channels today. “When thousands of people are following you and the media is looking at your forecasts so closely, you feel a great sense of responsibility,” he says. Direct feedback from a massive social media following holds his work accountable.

Rather than taking computerised simulations at face value, he rigorously filters model outputs through ground parameters, such as tracking wind farm dynamics to see if dry desert air from Rajasthan will disarm an approaching monsoon system over Sindh. He logs his prediction outcomes to calculate error margins and analyse why a forecast failed, aiming for a self-tracked accuracy rate of 85-90 pc.

Memon relies on earnings from an entirely unrelated livelihood to fund the operations: a small business specialising in CCTV surveillance and security equipment. He funnels the profits into his forecasting work, paying for expensive subscriptions to premium global weather models, including the Global Forecast System, the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts, and ICON, along with deploying a handful of private weather stations in Karachi.

Junaid Yamin, the CEO of Weatherwalay, also has no formal background in meteorology. He took a corporate and technological route, building a private network of around 400 weather stations across Pakistan. They combine real-time data from these physical stations with high-resolution imagery from the European Weather Satellite (EUMETSAT). Their software pipeline ingests and synthesises 10 international weather models simultaneously, using proprietary machine-learning algorithms to track trend patterns over 10 to 14 day horizons. When an anomaly is detected, the platform translates raw synoptic data into alerts that are sent to mobile apps as push notifications.

Weatherwalay employs dedicated AI/ML software engineers whose sole function is to test prediction accuracy and continuously train machine-learning models against ground-truth data from their nationwide stations.

Us vs Them

Us…

Sarfaraz says that sensationalism often fuels private weather pages. “I have observed that they create a lot of unnecessary hype,” he says. “In Karachi’s case specifically, the climate event is usually not as big as it is exaggerated online. Maybe they’re concerned about the likes and followers on their Facebook pages.”

If an independent forecaster makes a correct call, Sarfaraz argues the credit should go to the global models, not the institutions or individuals themselves. He argues this, saying that independent forecasters rely on freely available global datasets without possessing their own physical observation networks, Doppler radars, or upper-air radiosonde feeds.

Rasul, however, acknowledges that while independent forecasters may lack formal degrees in atmospheric sciences, repeated practice and passion have honed their skills, and they fill a vacuum left by PMD’s communication shortcomings.

He recalls recent discussions with an Indian Meteorological Department (IMD) official, who confessed that private digital giants like AccuWeather and Weather Underground are giving state forecasters a run for their money, compelling the IMD to aggressively upgrade its modeling and delivery mechanisms. There might be something to learn from here.

“In a way, it is a positive sign that private weather forecasters are entering the field and competing with national services,” he says. “Currently, the way PMD simply issues long lists of cities across a province where significant weather events rarely happen is hardly effective forecasting. This needs to improve.”

Them…

The tension between state meteorologists and independent analysts often descends into public turf wars. Private weather firecasters argue that these kinds of standoffs leave the public stranded in a dangerous information vacuum.

Memon says that the solution is not to undermine the state’s formal mandate, but to dismantle the barriers that keep private innovators at arm’s length. He points to international precedents of national meteorological agencies nurturing independent analysts with shared data pipelines and subsidised equipment.

He proposes that the government establish a formal, collaborative umbrella for both worlds. The PMD holds the statutory authority and access to multi-million-dollar Doppler radars, but real-world experience, local monitoring, and agility are what modern forecasting demands. When an institution isolates itself from that partnership, it is the country’s farmers, commuters, and urban residents who bear the cost of an institutional divide.

Yamin frames the challenge not as a lack of talent or infrastructure, but an entrenched culture of running administrative silos. Every department and startup tries to reinvent the wheel rather than leverage existing capabilities across public and private lines. Climate specialist Daniel Cull stressed that climate change is a mammoth crisis that neither the public sector, private enterprise, nor non-profits can tackle alone. The World Meteorological Organisation has long advocated for institutionalised public-private engagement precisely because unpredictable weather requires both deep scientific infrastructure and nimble, tech-driven delivery systems.

Yamin, in PMD’s defence, says that the public and media must recognise that atmospheric science is probabilistic. He suggests that official forecasters must frame predictions accurately, communicating likelihoods instead of absolutes, and updating the public continuously as initial parameters evolve.

But collaboration is only half the battle.

To environmental lawyer Ahmad Rafay Alam, the reality that ordinary Pakistanis suffer the brunt of climate disasters only because information is not given in time is the real tragedy. The data exists. The alerts are sent. The breakdown happens because of downstream governance.

“We knew on Friday, July 24, for example, that it was going to rain on the weekend and that there was going to be urban flooding in Lahore and Gujranwala based on a PMD flood forecasting notification issued at 12:10 PM,” he says. “These are official notifications that go to everyone.”

Alam turns to apps such as Weatherwalay for alerts, though accessing wider geographic data requires a subscription. When assessing cross-border hydrology, he sidesteps official channels entirely. “I sometimes jump on my VPN to monitor flood data on Indian websites, as our transboundary river systems and shared geography mean upstream conditions directly affect our own.”

But a vulnerable farmer or katchi abadi dweller has neither a subscription nor guaranteed electricity. That is precisely why Provincial Disaster Management Authorities and district administrations exist. “The disaster management authorities have published a Multi-Hazard Vulnerability Risk Assessments for every district across the provinces,” says Alam. It maps out every threat, fire, drought, floods, and details exactly which infrastructure will be compromised. It’s all published, it’s all online. “I’ve seen whole volumes of it. So it is not a lack of data,” he says. “It’s a question of how you respond to it and get it into the hands of people who lack the equipment and information to protect themselves.”

Nowhere was this dysfunction more glaring than in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa last year. Monsoonal belts tracked unusually north, unleashing catastrophic flash floods across Swat and the valleys while all five rivers in Punjab swelled simultaneously.

Meanwhile, state departments squabbled.

“Last year there was a fight about what the definition of a flash flood is,” Alam recalls. The PMD argued that these rains didn’t fit the classic technical definition—X volume of water falls in Y amount of time. “This kerfuffle was a bit childish.”

In jagged mountain topography, where evacuating communities across gorges is a race against time, rigid meteorological pedantry costs lives. The PMD shouldn’t get bogged down in textbook legalities; it must issue immediate operational alerts to local administrations that a deadly threat is barrelling their way.

Alam is equally quick to push back against scapegoating the PMD for disasters engineered on the ground. In Swat, the wreckage left behind by raging waters exposed systemic governance failures that no radar system could fix.

There is a law in KP—Rivers Protection Ordinance, 2002—which says it is absolutely prohibited to build anything within 150 feet of the high-water mark of any river. “Now you tell me: what have people been doing on riverbanks for over two decades since that law came in? Building continuously,” says Alam. “How is that the PMD’s fault? The blame lies squarely with the local administrations.”

He gives the infamous example of the New Honeymoon Hotel in Kalam which was washed away in 2010, and again in 2022. They rebuilt it each time.

Advanced radar and private analytics can pinpoint the exact minute the deluge arrives, but until district officials act on incoming alerts, enforce zoning laws, and translate data into sirens for people, the country will keep describing every climate tragedy as an inevitable “act of God” instead of one that should hold humans accountable in government.

The cost of delayed forecasts

When the sky ruptured over Buner last year, Salim Khan, a journalist, was at home in Pacha Killay. Before his eyes, the Pir Baba bazaar—the valley’s economic spine—was swallowed whole. From the third floor, Khan watched charpoys, cars, goats, dissolve. “I saw human bodies being swept away,” he says. “I was recording these scenes for my television channel, but even a journalist behind the camera is, after all, only human. I found myself unable to hold back the tears.”

On the flat roof of a submerged school, a cluster of children huddled. Roads were severed, leaving neighbours to haul the injured in their own pickup trucks. At a hospital, the death toll escalated so fast that basic supplies ran out.

“There were not enough kafans (burial shrouds),” says Khan. Announcements were made from mosques after which people began arriving at the hospital with shrouds from their own homes. Among the dead was a mother still clasping her infant to her chest, later laid to rest together in a single grave.

The survivors said they had only heard broad forecasts of seasonal rain, the kind of advisories routinely issued across bureaucratic channels, but nothing that actually explained what could happen.

The PMD’s broad-strokes are designed for regional summaries. Agile independent forecasters often spot convective spikes on satellite feeds but their apparatus does not have the integrated, hyper-localised distribution channels required to translate warnings into sirens on the ground. And till this gap is narrowed, deadly waters will continue to fill it.

item.title: Rizvi: Gas supply to normalize by September second week
item.description:
BNP Acting Secretary General Ruhul Kabir Rizvi on Tuesday said normal gas supply across the country is expected to be restored by the first or second week of September.
He made the comments while talking to reporters after paying homage and offering prayers at the graves of BNP founder and late president Ziaur Rahman and former prime minister Khaleda Zia at Sher-e-Bangla Nagar in Dhaka on Tuesday morning.
Rizvi said Bangladesh has also been affected by the ongoing global energy crisis, particularly due to the US-Iran war and disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.
“This is a global crisis. Ships cannot come through the Strait of Hormuz because of the US-Iran war and fuel supplies are being disrupted. When one or two ships tried to come, bombs were dropped there,” he said.
He said Prime Minister Tarique Rahman is taking measures to address the energy crisis, allocating Tk40,000 crore from the budget for the energy and power sector to resolve the gas shortage.
Referring to the technical problems at the Floating Storage and Regasification Unit (FSRU) in Maheshkhali, Rizvi said repairs have already been completed and regasification has begun.
“Regasification has now started. Normal gas supply will be ensured by the first or second week of September, and electricity will also be available. We are already seeing some indications of that,” he said.
Speaking about BNP’s founding anniversary, Rizvi said the party believes in politics based on fulfilling its commitments to people.
He said BNP has come to power through a free and fair election and Prime Minister Tarique Rahman has been working tirelessly, day and night, to fulfil the pledges made to the people after taking office.
On the challenges facing the party and government, Rizvi said there are various challenges, conspiracies and plots, but Tarique Rahman is leading the government while confronting them.
“If there were no challenges, there would be no credit in overcoming them and achieving something good,” he said.
Rizvi said the government is also working to implement BNP’s commitments, including the Farmers Card, Family Card and allowances for imams and muezzins.
Asked about the apparent overlap between the party and the government, as BNP is a political party while the government is a separate entity, Rizvi termed the question an “ambiguous term.”
“The people voted for the party, and the party formed the government. The ministers in the government are BNP leaders. Most of them are BNP leaders. So when the people voted for and elected the party, its members will naturally run the government,” he said.
He said BNP had repeatedly made it clear that its leaders and activists, from grassroots members to the national level, were part of the government’s broader effort.
“Our leaders and activists will properly inform the people about all government programmes being implemented for public welfare and in the public interest. There is no contradiction in this,” Rizvi said.
He stressed that the party and government remain separate entities, but the responsibility of running the government lies with BNP and its leaders.

America Is Buying an Army It Cannot Command
item.description:
The U.S. Army has committed to a million small drones by 2028. The Department of Defense has not decided who will authorize how they fire.

That is not a materiel gap. The volume is on order; Nvidia’s latest earnings guidance says the compute to run it is on the way. It is a governance gap, and it is now the single largest exposure in the American national security posture entering the fourth quarter of 2026.

Consider what landed inside a seventy-two-hour window this week. On Tuesday, Nvidia posted $96.2 billion in second-quarter revenue, with $89 billion of it in the data-center segment and guided to $108 billion in the September quarter — an annualized run rate through American hyperscalers of more than $400 billion, the largest defense-adjacent capital cycle in modern history. The same day, Boeing, Lockheed Martin, and RTX filed their responses to the Deputy Defense Secretary’s twenty-one-day production ultimatum on accelerated interceptor delivery. Nine days earlier, the Pentagon had opened the vendor portal for the $185 billion Golden Dome missile-defense program.

The chips are being funded. The primes are being pushed. The perimeter is being paid for. None of it tells you who decides when a fielded drone force pushes beyond its vendor’s safety rails during a live engagement.

That is not a hypothetical. Since March, the Department of Defense has formally designated Anthropic — the American AI lab whose Claude model is in active use within U.S. Defense environments — a “supply chain risk.” The two sides opened arguments in DC court over the blacklisting on May 19. In May, the Department expanded its classified AI work to eight companies, explicitly excluding Anthropic. On February 28, OpenAI took the other side of the same question, signing a deal to run its models on a Pentagon classified network. The day before, more than 580 Google employees, including DeepMind researchers, signed an open letter urging Google’s CEO to refuse the same kind of arrangement.

The industrial base of American artificial intelligence is not aligned on whether it will perform the classified work the drone doctrine assumes. The Pentagon’s response has been to fund compute, sign one lab, blacklist a second, and litigate.

Picture April 2027. A deployed American drone force is airborne over a contested Indo-Pacific corridor. A vendor safety guardrail on the targeting AI refuses a strike within a sixty-second window. The commander needs an override. No office at the Department of Defense — including the Chief Digital and AI Officer — holds explicit arbitration authority between the vendor’s guardrail and the commander’s judgment at operational tempo. The decision will be made ad hoc, by whichever lawyer or flag officer picks up the phone.

That is the arbitration gap. It is not the debt-service bill. It is not the interceptor shortfall. It is not even the shipbuilding backlog. It is the fact that the United States is standing up the largest defense-adjacent capital cycle in modern history — Golden Dome’s $185 billion, a million-drone target by 2028, and $1 billion for 340,000 attritable systems by 2027 — with no institutional authority designated to arbitrate how any of it fires. It is a supervisory function no institution has yet been chartered to perform, and no doctrine has yet been written to describe it.

Beijing runs the inverse problem. Paul Scharre laid out the industrial-base half of this argument in “Losing the War of the Future,” published in Foreign Affairs on June 23. What his piece understates is the demand side: even if the United States builds the drones, the doctrine and civil-military arbitration required to employ them do not yet exist at scale. The People’s Liberation Army’s answer is on the record. Three PLA researchers — Lieutenant Colonels Li Hengrui and Wang Haiyuan and Senior Colonel Cheng Jinming — published “all-domain megacity incapacitation warfare” in Military Art, the Central Military Commission’s restricted journal, in March 2025. Nathan Beauchamp-Mustafaga and Andrew Wang brought the article into the English-language conversation this summer in “Total War on Taipei,” published in War on the Rocks. The concept identifies the operational meaning of Xi Jinping’s “national total war” as an integrated arbitration architecture that fuses military, civilian, media, and party assets under a single narrative apparatus.

The PLA may struggle to execute it. The Central Military Commission, which began this term with seven members, has been reduced to two, hollowed out by disciplinary investigations. But the design is on the page. The American design is not.

Three signals will indicate by year-end whether the gap is closing or widening.

First, does the CDAO’s office designate a named override authority for wartime AI lab guardrails? Second, is the Anthropic-DoD blacklisting resolved into a joint framework for classified use, or does the litigation calcify? Third, does the FY27 defense-authorization conference name a joint force to operate Golden Dome, or fund the program without operator language? As of this week, all three are moving the wrong way.

The next war will not be lost because America bought the wrong drone. It will be lost because America bought the right one and never decided who could tell it to fire.

item.title: The Cultural Roots of Strategic Surprise and Resilience: the Israeli case of October 2023
item.description:
October 7th, 2023, 06:29 AM. Probably the most tragic day in Israel’s history. A surprise attack conducted by Hamas from the Gaza Strip caught Israel completely off guard. Hamas terrorists infiltrated Israel, killing more than 1200 Israelis and abducting more than 250 individuals into the Gaza Strip. They exercised mass murder and rape, effectively conquering parts of Israel’s Western Negev for several hours. This was a colossal military and intelligence failure, more dramatic than that of the Yom Kippur War in 1973. It was also, of course, a policy failure. The core foundations of Israel’s security doctrine – defense, early warning, and deterrence – completely shattered.

How could this happen to the Israeli Defense Forces (IDF), one of the best militaries in the world, and to one of the best intelligence communities in the world? For me, as a brigadier general in the Israeli Defense Intelligence (IDI) reserves with decades of practical experience, and as a scholar of Israeli strategic culture and intelligence culture, this was a puzzle. Almost inconceivable. I was surprised by the magnitude of Israel’s surprise. How could Israel’s security establishments reach October 7th with their “eyes wide shut” about Hamas intentions and capabilities?

But as the regional war which followed October 2023 commenced, I recognized another interesting puzzle. Israeli security establishments have, writ large, recovered from the failure of October 2023, with Israel fighting for almost three years in several fronts, from the Gaza Strip to Iran. Although not gaining “total victory”, these establishments reached impressive operational achievements. They dismantled most of Hamas’ military and civilian infrastructure in the Gaza Strip and eliminated most of Hamas leadership in the Middle East; dismantled most of Hizballah assets in Lebanon, while also eliminating Hizballah leader Nasrallah, and demoralizing Hizballah in the famous pagers operation; destroyed many of the Houthi assets in Yemen; and in June 2025 and March 2026, conducted unprecedented attacks in Iran, including the elimination of Iran’s Supreme Leader and most of Iran’s military leadership, and degrading Iran’s nuclear and military capabilities.

How could the same establishments, which colossally failed to prevent the Hamas attack in October 2023, reach such achievements during 2024 and 2025? How could an intelligence system completely surprised by Hamas allow Israel to completely surprise Iran, the regional super-power? How could Israel “turn the tides” of the war after October 2023, and then, like the Phoenix from Greek mythology, “rise from the ashes” and conduct phenomenal strikes in Iran?

These are the topics I discuss in my new book, which reveals the cultural roots of Israel’s strategic surprise in October 2023, and of Israeli resilience following October 2023. The book knowingly focuses on Israel’s security establishments, and not on Israeli policy makers. Its scope is limited, and its conclusions will naturally be debated.

I open the book by acknowledging that some of my previous insights, which characterized Israeli intelligence culture prior to October 2023, were wrong. For instance, I assessed that this culture relies on professional norms and values of critical thinking, a sense of individual responsibility, and moral courage in the face of hierarchy. October 7th, unfortunately, showed that some of these remained aspirational norms rather than realized behavior in Israel’s security establishments.

Several typical facets of Israeli strategic and intelligence cultures account for both failure and success. For instance, the Israeli typical focus on operational, tactical, and targeting intelligence prior to October 7th resulted in an under-appreciation for strategic analysis, military analysis, and strategic early warning from war. The low quality of these disciplines was one of the factors for the October 7th failure. But the inclination towards targeting intelligence, and the close integration of intelligence into decision-making and operations, also enabled Israel to conduct ground-breaking overt and covert operations across the Middle East, relying on high-resolution and real-time targeting intelligence. Many more examples are discussed in the book.

However, the book stresses that strategic culture and intelligence culture are not unitary in essence, nor are they fixed in time. Changes in these cultures can be caused by trauma, or by competition for dominance between sub-cultures. For instance, in the years prior to October 7th, hubris evolved in Israeli security establishments, which not just underestimated Hamas, but also overestimated their own military and intelligence capabilities. October 7th, naturally, created a post-traumatic effect. Israeli deterrence-oriented security doctrine, which was dominant prior to October 7th, became heavily oriented towards prevention after October 7th, not just regarding adversary nuclear projects. This “move between extremes”, or “over-adaptation”, is for itself typical of Israeli strategic culture.

In conclusion, the book applies the frameworks of strategic culture and intelligence culture to a real-world case of security performance. This perspective does not only apply to Israel. In the US, for instance, it can allow critical introspection of the recent conflict with Iran, including the repeated experienced surprise the US seems to be experiencing. Furthermore, understanding partners’ and allies’ cultures, and not just adversary ones, is an imperative. Especially for American scholars and practitioners. The book makes an important contribution to this perspective. At the end of the day, national security is all about people. Society and culture play a major role.

item.title: Two tankers carrying Saudi oil attacked in Strait of Hormuz
item.description:
By Florence Tan

item.title: Muneeba hails 'belief' after shaky Pakistan trounce Thailand in Women's Asia Cup
item.description:
DUBAI: Pakistan opener Muneeba Ali hailed the team’s “belief” after the side endured a chaotic batting show to trounce Thailand in their Women’s Asia Cup opener at the Dubai International Cricket Stadium on Tuesday night.

Pakistan’s batting woes exposed themselves once again as they were reduced to 23-3 within the powerplay after captain Fatima Sana won the toss. However, wicket-keeper-batter Muneeba stabilised the innings, and dug in to produce a sturdy knock of 54 runs off 52 balls that gave Pakistan a 35-run win.

Muneeba provided some much-needed relief to the batting line-up, braving the hot and humid conditions in Dubai.

“When wickets kept falling in the powerplay, we knew if we got a good partnership and kept on scoring runs, it would put the bowlers under pressure, and give us opportunities to score,” she said in the post-match press conference.

“That’s what my strategy was.” the bespectacled southpaw added, when asked about how she navigated the innings.

“In the past, if wickets fell in the powerplay, we wouldn’t be able to come back into the match.

“Today the difference was that even when we lost wickets, the team kept belief and tried setting a total which would be defendable against the opposition on this pitch.”

Pakistan’s propensity for batting collapses cost them greatly in the Women’s T20 World Cup in June, where they managed only one win in their group, against the Netherlands.

A lack of momentum and frequent collapses led them to humbling 64 and 113-run losses against India and Australia respectively, while a mid-innings stutter against Bangladesh left the team at 100-8, unable to chase an achievable 124.

The bilateral series that followed against Sri Lanka proved to be better from a batting perspective, especially with a new opening pair in Muneeba and Shawal Zulfiqar. However, the line-up still came up short, as Sri Lanka chased both targets of 170-odd in the first two matches to take the series.

“Obviously, in the last few T20 series we played before the Sri Lanka, our batting unit did not click as such and we had our struggles,” said Muneeba.

“We have been working on those issues in camps, to make sure we don’t repeat the same mistakes, and bring in some different options in our batting.”

Pakistan had found themselves in trouble early on, faltering at 6-2 at the two-over mark after a double wicket maiden by Thipatcha Phuttawong.

After a stodgy powerplay, Muneeba and Sadaf Shamas set about a rebuild, stitching a 54-run partnership to ease the early-innings jitters. Shamas, trying to cut a wider delivery, fell for a run-a-ball 2o. Fatima, who has been reliable with the bat in recent times, fell for a duck in the same over to put Pakistan in a real spot of bother.

Muneeba reached her half-century in the 15th over. Though a flurry of late wickets blotted the flow of runs, Muneeba’s knock and a useful cameo of 12 not out off four balls by Tuba Hassan took Pakistan to a first-innings score of 119-9.

Muneeba said after the match that though the team had aimed to put up a score of at least 140 on the board, they knew that 120 or 130-plus would be defendable by the team’s bowling line-up.

Spin trap

And defend they did; skipper Fatima was validated for her choice of batting first as Pakistan reduced Thailand to 84-8 for their 20 overs, owing to an expert spin-strangle.

Sadia Iqbal took a double wicket maiden of her own as Thailand found themselves at 6-2 at the two-over mark, mirroring Pakistan’s position at the corresponding point in their own innings.

The next 11 overs then amounted to only 37 runs as Pakistan’s spin attack tightened their grip on the match with disciplined bowling, giving nothing away to the batters.

Chasing 120,Thailand were 42-4 at the 13th over mark, requiring almost 12 runs an over thereon.

Nashra Sandhu’s introduction after the powerplay proved key with the veteran conceding only six runs across her four overs, she picked up the wicket of Natthakan Chantham with an excellent flighted delivery that turned to miss the bat and smash the off-stump.

“I didn’t have any complicated plans,” said Nashra in a post-match reflection video posted on Pakistan Cricket Board’s social media handles, featuring her and team-mate Tuba Hassan.

“I knew there was bounce and turn in the pitch, and that it was keeping low. I just had to bowl at the right spots, the pitch did the rest.”

Tuba had a decisive all-round impact on the match, featuring her emphatic stint with the bat and two wickets for 17 runs in her four overs. In the field, she nailed a direct-hit with razor-sharp accuracy to run Naomi Hamilton out.

“My plan was simple; bowl wicket-to-wicket and vary the pace as much as possible, because we also need to prepare for the next match,” said Tuba.

She added that the conditions were very humid, making them a little “tricky”, as the ball would slip easily.

“These are exactly the things we need to learn from, so that we can make less mistakes in the next matches and play better.”

For Thailand, the defeat marked the end of their Asia Cup campaign, having already played their first two group-stage matches that ended in a win against Hong Kong and a drubbing at the hands of India.

With first points on the board, Pakistan now turn their attention to the ever-crucial fixture against arch-rivals India on Saturday.

item.title: Act for Nutrition conference: Expert says malnutrition underfunded despite ‘catastrophic consequences’
item.description:
A two-day international conference, ‘Act For Nutrition: The Emergency We Can No Longer Ignore’, is being held at Islamabad’s Serena Hotel on Pakistan’s persistent nutrition and stunting crisis.

With more than 40 per cent of children under five stunted, a maternal mortality rate of 155 deaths per 100,000 live births, and malnutrition costing Pakistan upwards of $17 billion annually, the country stands at a crossroads: continue on the current trajectory and surrender an entire generation’s potential, or choose a different future.

The two-day conference is bringing together policymakers, international development leaders, health professionals and nutrition experts to confront the burgeoning crisis and build momentum for urgent, coordinated action.

The focus of discussions will be on moving the national conversation beyond statistics towards practical, measurable interventions that can improve nutrition outcomes and protect Pakis­tan’s human capital and future generations.

View the full agenda here.

4:38pm - Researcher explains why ‘1,000-day’ period is critical to addressing malnutrition

Director of the International Research Force Dr Hana Mahmood explained why the first 1,000-day period of an infant’s life remained critical in addressing malnutrition.

“The most important thing we have to attend to right now is that these 1,000 days are those days in which growth is exponentially high and the requirement for micronutrients is massive,” Dr Mahmood said.

She added that during this time, the immune system and major organs were developing in such a way that any lack in nutritional input could lead to irreversible damage.

“During the first two years of life, 80pc of a child’s brain develops,” she said. Dr Mahmood also noted that Pakistan had one of the highest child-under-five mortality rates, a majority of which was contributed by malnutrition.

“250m deaths can be averted by focusing on prevention of stunting,” she said.

4:27pm - Session titled ‘First 1,000 days: Why women and girls matter for nutrition’ begins

4:10pm - Agri consultant highlights need for demand pull in producing nutritionally rich food

Agriculture consultant Hasan Khurrum Hanif, talking about producing nutritionally dense food, said, “Pakistani farmers need a demand pull, rather than a supply push”.

“Farmers will produce what you pay us to produce and if there is a market where I can sell zinc-fortified wheat, where I can sell vegetables with lower pesticide residue, all of those require a different input package, which has a cost component,” he said.

Hanif added that processors needed to provide farmers an ecosystem.

3:55pm - Food safety infrastructure critical for nutrition, economy, says Tetra Pak executive

Corporate Affairs Director at Tetra Pak Noor Aftab stressed the significance of food safety, saying that “food systems need to be treated as critical infrastructure”.

He said that Pakistan is one of the largest milk-producing countries, but there were no safe milk or pasteurisation laws in the country, depriving the economy of $30bn export potential.

He added that in Pakistan, milk is taxed at one of the highest rates in the world. “If there is a resilient food systems infrastructure built within Pakistan, coupled with sustainable fiscal roadmaps… that will allow […] the infrastructure to act as a catalyst for nourishment and improvement.”

3:45pm - Nutrition investment reduced absenteeism rate in Bangladesh, says official

Project Manager at the Workforce Nutrition GM Reza Sumon, joining the conference through video conference from Bangladesh, discussed nutrition investments for the workforce.

He said that in Bangladesh’s government sector, the anaemia rate within the workforce was at 51.9pc. However, after interventions via funding for fortified rice, oils and iron and folic acid tablets, the anaemia rate dropped to 32pc, Sumon said, which helped convince the private sector to make similar investments in nutrition.

He said after the private sector invested $10m in nutrition in the past year, absenteeism in workplaces has reduced from 70pc to 40pc.

3:40pm - EBM executive shares details on a fortified biscuits initiative

Head of Corporate Communications & Sustainability at English Biscuit Manufacturers (EBM) Attiyah Inaam Khan shared details of an initiative launched by the company in which fortified biscuits were provided to mothers to address malnutrition.

“We tracked them for five years, and mothers who received biscuits showed great iron levels during pregnancy, and children born under the study showed stronger cognitive development,” she recalled.

“It is not about margins but more about whether there is evidence on the ground and whether the intervention can be scalable,” she added.

“Government can also play a very important lever here: tax credit for fortification in products and reduce the import duty on fortification,” she added.

3:36pm - Session on mobilising private capital and partnerships begins

A panel discussion on mobilising private capital and partnerships has begun.

3:12pm - ADB views malnutrition as an economic issue, working with BISP, says official

Senior Project Officer at Asian Development Bank (ADB) Mansoor Ali Masood said the bank was looking at malnutrition through an economic lens rather than viewing it solely as a health issue.

“Hence, we are trying to mainstream it through social protection, education, agriculture and water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) services,” he said, adding that ADB was supporting the Benazir Nashonuma Programme and had allocated around half of a $960m fund to address stunting.

“ADB is supporting the expansion of BNP, helping BISP in expanding the awareness of mothers who are better informed and can take better decisions for their children and ensure dietary diversity.”

3:07pm - ‘Nutrition is part of human capital’

The Dean of Research at Pakistan Institute of Development Economics (PIDE) Dr Shujaat Farooq, said that the economic cost of malnutrition was “too much”.

Citing statistics, he said 40pc of children in the country are facing stunting while 25 million children are out of school. He added that 75pc of children in schools were unable to learn proficiently due to malnutrition.

“Nutrition is part of human capital,” Farooq said.

3:00pm - No multi-sectoral nutrition programmes in the past decade: Planning ministry official

Chief of nutrition at the planning ministry, Dr Nazeer Ahmed, said in the past “one to two decades, there had been no major nutrition programme implemented in the provinces, except the Benazir Nashonuma Programme”.

“We have the policies in the four provinces, and nutrition strategies [..] But on the ground, we do not have any multi-sectoral programmes implemented,” he said.

2:55pm - Nutrition not often framed as GDP statistic: Gates Foundation official

Gates Foundation Senior Programme Officer of Development Policy and Finance Dr Ammar Malik said that according to World Bank statistics, for every dollar a government invested in nutrition, it could get up to $23 back in the form of economic benefits.

Questioning why such a high return on investment was still ignored, Malik said one of the issues was that nutrition investments were long-term, with returns becoming obvious years or decades later.

He added another issue was that nutrition is seen as a standalone topic in such discussions, instead of framing it as a gross domestic product statistic.

“If I were to say to you that Pakistan is losing 3pc of its GDP because of lack of investment in nutrition, that is a much stronger argument for economic policymakers than it is to talk about nutrition,” he said.

2:50pm - Gates Foundation official says Pakistan’s crisis is a ‘balance sheet problem’

Gates Foundation’s Dr Ammar Malik, who serves as the senior programme officer of development policy and finance, said the nutrition problem in Pakistan was a “balance sheet problem”.

“The government of Pakistan can either now decide to spend more on nutrition today through our budgets, or we can pay the price of this lack of investment in the form of lost gross domestic product over the next several years or even decades,” he said.

2:45pm — ‘Nutrition has few dedicated champions’

Global Alliance for Improved Nutrition Executive Director Lawrence Haddad noted that another reason nutrition was underfunded was a lack of dedicated efforts towards the issue.

“Why is this? Well, because malnutrition is multi-sectoral. It is the interaction of poor diet, poor water, poor sanitation, poor healthcare, and poor care in general, and so each of these areas has its own ministry.”

“There is no ministry of nutrition,” he added.

2:42pm — Expert says malnutrition underfunded despite ‘catastrophic consequences’

The session on investing in nutrition began with a video note by Global Alliance for Improved Nutrition Executive Director Lawrence Haddad, who pointed out that malnutrition remained underfunded “despite its catastrophic impact”.

“Forty five per cent of children’s deaths under three worldwide are due to malnutrition,” Haddad noted, adding that less than 1pc of international aid was spent on malnutrition.

“It is quite invisible in many ways,” he added.

2:30pm — Conference resumes after lunch break

1:50pm - Lunch break

The conference will resume at 2:30pm.

1:40pm- WHO official says ‘no bigger risk than lack of action’

Ellen Thom, the deputy representative for the World Health Organisation Pakistan warned that “there was no bigger risk than the lack of action” in addressing malnutrition.

“As we speak, before I finish answering, [..] in the next three minutes, at least 14 children will have died across the world from causes related to maternal and child malnutrition,” Thom said, adding that such deaths were preventable and “we cannot afford not to take action”.

She also noted that Pakistan was suffering an annual economic loss of $17bn due to stunting and malnutrition.

1:34pm - WFP official says malnutrition not just driven by poverty

Thomas Conan, the deputy country director for the World Food Programme, said that malnutrition was not just driven by poverty.

“It is also directly influenced and fed by poor access to services … health services and water and sanitation services,” he said.

1:15pm - Expert calls for focusing on adolescent nutrition

Food security adviser on nutrition and social protection at GIZ Pakistan, Dr Faiza Wahab, raised the alarm at the “missing adolescent middle” during conversations about malnutrition.

She said that nutrition discourse had been focused on the first 1,000 days of a child, but she stressed, “we are really missing the middle, which is between childhood and motherhood”.

“Focusing on adolescent nutrition is not to prepare them for motherhood, but it is also a window where the investment really returns in the form of human capital development,” she said.

She explained that during adolescent years, young girls were vulnerable to anaemia and iron deficiencies due to “rapid growth, hormonal changes and menstruation”.

“If she is not empowered, she cannot participate in education, and she has less cognitive capabilities,” Dr Wahab said.

1:10pm - WHO official stresses need for integrating social protection programmes with health services

Ellen Thom, the deputy representative for the World Health Organisation Pakistan, said integrating social protection with existing health and nutrition services is important.

She said that evidence showed that doing so and strengthening integrated primary healthcare was an effective way of reaching vulnerable families and delivering high-impact nutrition interventions.

1:02pm - WFP official says nutrition is not just about food

Thomas Conan, the deputy country director for the World Food Programme, said that nutrition was not only about food.

“It’s not only about access to food. It is about a healthy diet, the capacity to ensure multi-sectoral intervention and collaboration among us,” he said.

He said that it was also necessary to ensure access to a more healthy diet and the design of the social protection was nutrition-sensitive,” he said.

12:50pm - BISP official talks about Nashonuma programme

BISP Director General Dr Asim Ijaz spoke about the Benazir Nashonuma Programme (BNP), which he said had added a “nutritional and health layer” to the existing BISP registry.

He stressed that there exists a 1,000-day window for a child’s development, during which “irreversible damage can occur”.

“This is why BISP changed its thinking in 2019,” he said. He said that the recognition was then realised in the Nashonuma pilot launch in 2020, which was then phased out country-wide in 2021.

“Nashonuma itself is not a separate bureaucracy but layered onto existing platforms,” he said, explaining that BISP’s registry was now carrying a nutritional and health layer.

“So the idea was to have one beneficiary record with multiple beneficial layers,” he said.

12:42pm - ‘We can no longer afford to look away,’ BISP chairperson says

Senator Rubina Khalid, the chairperson of Benazir Income Support Programme, said in her keynote address that the responsibility lay not just with providing financial assistance, but with also helping families move from vulnerability towards dignity.

“We have gathered here today … because we can no longer afford to look away,” she said. She said that more than 40pc of children under five in Pakistan were stunted, while malnutrition placed a huge burden on the economy.

“Stunting is not only a health issue. It is a human capital issue, an economic issue and a challenge to Pakistan’s future,” she said. She said that the country lacked integration of the programmes it had to address these issues.

At the end of her address, she said: “We must work together so that every child in Pakistan has the opportunity to grow, learn and reach their full potential. Because every child we protect from malnutrition is not simply a life protected, it is the future protected, a family strengthened and a stronger Pakistan secured.”

12:40pm: Session on integrating nutrition into social protection systems begins

A session on integrating nutrition into social protection systems begins.

12:30pm - Sri Lankan doctor calls for understanding child growth trajectory in South Asia

Dr Rannan-Eliya, in answer to a question, pointed out that the child growth trajectory in South Asia was not the same as the rest of the world.

“We have sort of misunderstood the problem,” he remarked, adding: “There is no uniformity in child growth, and because we use a single growth standard, we partly misdiagnose what is going on”.

“In my sense, Sri Lankan kids need to be better nourished but there is a limit to what we can do and we need to understand that,” he said. He noted that a similar understanding was also being realised in India.

“So we need to do more as South and South East Asian countries, and it’s something that needs better investigation, and it is leading to a misunderstanding of what the problem is.”

12:13pm - Expert says nutrition an issue of human capital, economic growth

Dr Irshad Danish, the co-chair of the Global Nutrition Report Stakeholder Group, said that from his experience, Pakistan had low allocation, fragmented spending and implementation challenges.

“If we need $10 to feed malnourished children, we are spending only $2,” he said. He added that Pakistan was losing $17bn annually due to malnutrition.

He said that this also resulted in poor education outcomes, children with cognitive issues and lower workforce productivity.

“So, nutrition is not just a health issue. It is an issue of human capital and economic growth,” he said. He said that the cost of malnutrition was far greater than the cost of prevention.

“We need to move from fragmented spending towards strategic investment, and from hidden allocations to transparent budgets,” he said.

12:00pm - Doctor stresses importance of lady health workers

Co-chair of the Global Nutrition Report Stakeholder Group Dr Irshad Danish stressed the significance of the lady health workers programme.

“It was one of the strongest community based health workers model and its coverage was around 60pc, with over 100,000 lady health workers,” he said, adding that the workers enjoyed community ownership.

“These workers were often the first link of access for healthcare [..] many independent evaluation where these health workers were available, there was better health knowledge and better access to essential services.”

11:46am - Sri Lankan official explains how country scaled health systems

Dr Ravi Rannan-Eliya, the executive director of Sri Lanka’s Institute of Health Policy, said that 100 years ago, the South Asian country had worse health outcomes than the rest of the region.

“We were the sick man of South Asia, but now we have the best health plan. How did that happen? One simple reason I always tell people was the ballot box … the British decided to give self-rule,” he said.

He said that as a consequence, there was a pressure to give free education and to expand health services. He said that voters prioritised access to care over all other things.

11:42am - Session on South and South-East Asia’s current realities

The session on South and South-East Asia’s current realities has now begun.

11:30am- Scaling Up Nutrition movement official highlights its progress

Asia Regional Representative of the Scaling Up Nutrition (SUN) Movement Dr Srikanth Eadara spoke about the objectives of the movement, which he said was comprised of 67 countries and was a country-led global nutrition advocacy platform.

“It unites different stakeholders coming from civil society, private sector, donors, UN, agencies and other entities as well as youth to end malnutrition,” he said, adding that it was launched in 2013 to “ ensure a coordinated multisectoral and multi-stakeholder action to address malnutrition in all its forms”.

“We are currently in the fourth phase of the SUN Movement, and it is based on the current challenges and current context of nutrition, which shows that, yes, there is progress; however, the progress is slow and uneven,” he noted.

Dr Eadara also spoke of the issues surrounding nutrition finance, highlighting that the cost of malnutrition was “estimated to be around 5 to 11pc of the total GDPs of Asia and Africa”.

He warned that recent funding cuts, particularly in the World Health Organisation have “threatened to reverse progress” made on nutrition.

“The reduction will also result in increased hardships and deaths, with a lot of implications for public health and economic growth and stability,” he said.

11:25am - Doctor says nutrition the ‘outcome of many systems’

Dr Aminah Jahangir, the global lead for health and nutrition at the Aga Khan Foundation, said that nutrition is the outcome of many systems and cannot be solved by one. She said that climate was already shaping the conditions in which children grow.

“Our experience suggests that the outcomes are better where health services, food systems and community institutions have worked around the same household over many years. It reminds us that progress is achievable in our own context,” she said.

11:20am - Social protection can address malnutrition, says WFP official

The WFP official spoke of one of the three priorities the organisation held for its work in South Asia was advocacy for policy engagement.

She explained, “this is a continuous effort to work with governments from South Asia to highlight how social protection can be more than a safety net and more than a poverty reduction instrument”.

Hobbs said that with the right intentions, social protection held promise to improve nutrition, diets and address malnutrition.

“This is because social protection already reaches the families that are the most vulnerable and those are the families that face the highest challenges,” she added.

11:12am: WFP official says over 80pc of stunted children come from middle-income countries

Asia Pacific Regional Nutrition Adviser for the World Food Programme Nora Hobbs, in her address, spoke of the geographical realities of stunting, stating that the majority of children affected by stunting are from middle-income countries.

“Over 80pc of the world’s stunted children are in middle-income countries,” she said.

The WFP official continued: “This means that low-income countries may have the highest rate and prevalence, but because middle-income countries have such a large population, it may have higher numbers of stunted children.”

She stressed that the facts highlighted that stunting was a result of “inequalities within countries”.

11:05am - Expert highlights need for coordinated response

Dr Giacomo Zanello, an associate professor of Food Economics and Health at the University of Reading, said that neither food nor the health systems could solve malnutrition alone.

“Progress requires coordinated action across food systems, health systems and social protection. Countries that built integrated approaches before crisis struck, were able to keep essential services running through disruption,” he said.

“Integration cannot be improvised during a crisis. It has to be done in advance,” he said.

11:00am - Expert says 2.6bn people cannot afford a healthy diet

Dr Giacomo Zanello, an associate professor of Food Economics and Health at the University of Reading, presented a report on global nutrition.

“Around the world, progress on nutrition is under increasing pressure. Climate shocks, conflict, economic uncertainty … are affecting food and health systems,” he said.

He said that the 2026 global nutrition report focused on how countries can build healthy diets, through stronger integration of food and health systems while building resilience.

“Today, 2.6 billion cannot afford a healthy diet,” he said. He said that extreme weather, rising food prices and pressure on health services were arriving alongside conflict and instability, which was affecting food and health systems.

10:55am - Session on global and regional realities begins

The session on global and regional realities has now begun.

10:52am - UN official says nutrition should not be activated only after a crisis

Pernille Ironside, the United Nations’ resident coordinator in Pakistan, said that communities must be at the heart of the response to malnutrition and stunting.

“Investing in front line workers and community-based platforms and listening to communities themselves can strengthen the uptake of essential services and practices, reinforce local ownership and ensure that women and children most at risk are reached,” she said.

She said that Pakistan knew better than most how quickly climate disasters, economic shocks and displacement can undermine years of development programmes.

“Nutrition, therefore, cannot be something we activate only after a crisis. It needs to be built into the preparedness, into the anticipatory action and the shock responsive systems so that vulnerable families are identified beforehand,” she said.

10:46am - UN official says malnutrition an ‘emergency we can no longer ignore’

Pernille Ironside, the United Nations’ resident coordinator in Pakistan, said that malnutrition was an “emergency we can no longer ignore”.

“When we talk about nutrition, we are not only talking about what a child eats. We are talking about whether a child reaches their full potential. We are talking about the strength of Pakistan’s capital. Nutrition is not only a health issue, it’s a development issue, an economic issue and an issue of equity and opportunity,” she said.

She said that children living in poorer and remote areas were more likely to be left behind. She also said that at the same time, Pakistan faced a growing burden of obesity-related diseases.

10:40am - World Bank official says malnutrition barrier to health, prosperity of individuals, nations

Abigail Perry, the lead nutrition specialist at the World Bank, said malnutrition was a fundamental barrier to the health and prosperity of individuals, communities and nations.

“When a child’s development suffers early in life, the effects can last a lifetime,” she said. She said that the challenge for Pakistan was how to act at the scale, speed and quality required.

10:35am - WHO chief says nutrition is not just about food

World Health Organisation Director General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said nutrition was not only about food.

“It is about access to safe, healthy, diets and strong food systems. Government, academia, civil society and the private sector all have a role to play,” he said.

10:30am - WHO chief says malnutrition one of the greatest barriers to health, development and opportunity

World Health Organisation Director General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, in a recorded message, said that malnutrition remained one of the greatest barriers to health, development and opportunity.

“Every year, it contributes to millions of preventable deaths,” he said. He said that the problem was not a lack of knowledge, rather a lack of action.

10:20am - Minister says equity begins in the womb

Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal said that the Pakistan of 2047 is being built today.

“It is being built in the health of our mothers. It is being built in the nutrition of our infants. It is being built in our homes and communities and it is being built in the developing minds and bodies of our youngest children,” he said.

“We all have to work as a whole,” he said, calling for the conference to spur action.

“Let this be our commitment: every child nourished is protected, every child given a fair start brings Pakistan one step closer to the future we seek,” he said.

10:10am - Minister says investment in nutrition is not charity

“Pakistan cannot win the economic race of the 21st century if millions of children begin the race of life several steps behind than others. There can be no knowledge economy without developing the capacity of the human brain. There can be no productivity revolution without healthy and capable workers. There can be no genuine equality if inequality begins before a child is even born,” said Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal.

“Therefore, investment in nutrition is not charity, it is economic policy,” he said.

10:03am - Minister says first 5 years of a child’s life critical

Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal said that human resource development had not been prioritised in the past. He appreciated the initiative by DawnMedia Group to address the nutrition crisis and called on civil society to take up social issues.

“90 per cent of a children’s brain develops by the age of five .. so the first five years in the life of a child are the most critical,” he said.

“If we fail to develop that human infrastructure during the earliest years of life, we weaken every other investment we subsequently make,” he said.

“That is why stunting cannot remain merely a statistic. For the planning minister, it is a national development challenge,” he said.

9:57am - Planning minister says quality of human resource critical for countries

In his remarks, Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal, the chief guest, conveyed Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif’s firm commitment to addressing malnutrition and stunting as a national development priority.

He said that as the planning minister, he spent much of his time dealing with the architecture of Pakistan’s development.

“We discuss motorways, energy, dams and digital networks. All of these are essential, but there is one investment more fundamental than all others: the investment in human development,” he said.

“Ultimately it is humans and people who build nations. Therefore, the quality of human resource is critical for any country,” he said.

9:55am - Dawn CEO says nutrition crisis does not ‘look the same’ across the country

Dawn CEO Nazafreen Saigol Lakhani said the nutrition crisis did not “look the same in Tharparkar as it does in Chitral or in southern Punjab”, adding that the response could not be the same either.

“You will hear the economics of financing nutrition, the science of why children fail to grow even when food is technically available, and, I hope, the voices of the women and the mothers who carry the heaviest share of this burden and are so rarely asked to speak about it,” she said.

“With all those who have a role to play gathered around the same table, we have an opportunity to move from recognition of the scale of the problem towards urgent, coordinated and measurable action — action that can improve maternal and child nutrition, strengthen Pakistan’s human capital, and give future generations the opportunity to grow, learn and thrive,” she said.

“That is what this conference ultimately aims to achieve: to build a shared understanding of what needs to be done, and to begin charting a clear and practical roadmap for how we get there,” she added.

9:53am - Dawn CEO says nutrition not a problem for health ministry to solve alone

Dawn CEO Nazafreen Saigol Lakhani said that Pakistan loses close to $17 billion a year to the consequences of malnutrition, “more than what we typically borrow from the International Monetary Fund in any given year”.

“We spend enormous energy negotiating that borrowing. We spend comparatively little energy addressing a loss nearly as large, happening quietly, inside our own households,” she said.

“So this conference starts from a simple premise: nutrition is not a problem for a health ministry to solve alone. It sits at the intersection of health, agriculture, water, education, social protection, our economy and ultimately, our national security,” she added.

She said that countries such as Bangladesh, Peru, and Rwanda had demonstrated that stunting can be dramatically reduced within a generation, but “only when a nation decides, at the highest levels, that the future of its children is important enough to make it a collective priority”.

9:52am - Dawn CEO calls stunting crisis ‘a national emergency’

In her welcome remarks, Dawn CEO Nazafreen Saigol Lakhani said that four out of every ten children under the age of five in Pakistan were stunted.

“These are children whose physical growth and cognitive development may be permanently compromised – often before they have spoken their first words, entered a classroom or had the slightest chance to even dream of their own future,” she said.

“And when this is the reality for four out of every ten children in our country, we cannot merely call it a health problem. It is a national emergency – and a profound failure of our collective priorities,” she said.

9:45am - Conference begins

The conference has begun with the playing of the national anthem and the recitation of the Holy Quran.

item.title: US strike kills 5 and wounds dozens of civilians at a wedding, Iran says
item.description:
IRAN-CRISIS/USA-STRIKES

The US and Iran found themselves back in a war footing on Wednesday after the most significant exchange in weeks, with Washington threatening even more devastating strikes while Iran protested an attack that it said killed five and wounded dozens of civilians at a wedding.

The US military's Central Command said it completed a wave of strikes against Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps targets on Tuesday including air defense sites, radar systems, maritime assets and facilities, mine-laying capabilities, and communications sites.

Iranian media reported attacks on multiple targets around the country on Tuesday, many near the Strait of Hormuz, where Iran has been threatening oil tankers that dare transit the narrow waterway without authorisation.

Iran in turn said it struck US assets in Jordan and Iraq, according to official statements, while Iranian media reports said it also attacked Bahrain.

Although the IRGC said it killed a large number of US forces in Jordan, two US officials told Reuters there had not been any casualties, according to initial assessments.

Jordan's armed forces said its air defense systems dealt with 13 ballistic missiles that entered the kingdom's airspace, 10 of which were intercepted and three fell in remote areas. Bahrain said Iranian drones were intercepted and destroyed.

The IRGC also said its ground forces carried out combined missile and drone attacks on US bases in Erbil in northern Iraq, killing several US personnel. Neither Iraq nor the US had confirmed the attack.

The exchange of fire marked the first serious combat since July, ending a period in which the warring parties withheld fire but also showed little interest in returning to negotiations.

The lull came as the conflict appeared to be draining both sides. Iran's already ailing economy has been battered by war and its conventional military forces have been degraded.

Meanwhile, with US President Donald Trump confronting higher fuel prices ahead of November congressional elections, the US Army has used up much of its global stockpile of highly accurate long-range missiles, Reuters reported last month, raising concerns about the military's readiness for future conflicts.

Nonetheless, the renewal of hostilities produced another exchange of defiant statements.

"I like our position now much better, with almost total control of the Hormuz Strait, and their economy totally collapsing," Trump said. "They are just playing out the inevitable. When are the Iranian people going to rise up and fight?"

Iran threatened the US and its allies.

"We warn that the continuation of American evil in the region will be met with heavier, more widespread, and devastating responses, and any country that cooperates with the aggressive American army must accept its dangerous consequences," Iran's joint military command said in a statement.

Five killed at wedding

In what could be one of the more significant cases of civilian casualties in the war, five people were killed and 50 wounded at a wedding near Sirik, a coastal area on the Strait of Hormuz, the Iranian Red Crescent reported.

The Mehr news agency said a 4-year-old child was among those killed, while the IRNA news agency, citing a provincial official, put the number of wounded at 68.

US officials have yet to comment on the incident.

"This cruelty cannot be separated from the chain of atrocities that preceded it," Iran's foreign ministry spokesperson said in a statement, citing incidents including the blast at a school in Minab that killed 160 peopleat a girls' school on the first day of the war.

The Pentagon has yet to issue an official finding on the Minab strike, but it may have been the ‌result of US use of outdated targeting data, two sources familiar with the matter told Reuters.

The foreign ministry statement pledged that Iran would respond to "these savage crimes with firmness."

"Those governments and international institutions that remain silent in the face of such barbarism, or seek to justify such acts, must understand that their silence is not neutrality," Iran said. "Those who remain silent today will not be immune to its consequences tomorrow."
